title: Comments and Limited Protest of Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin in response to American Transmission Company LLC's 07/24/2026 tariff filing under ER26-3265.

documents.name: CUB Comments and Protest ER26-3265_final.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                                )
American Transmission Company LLC                               )          Docket No. ER26-3265
                                                                )

  COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST OF THE CITIZENS UTILITY BOARD OF
                          WISCONSIN

       The Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin (“Wisconsin CUB” or “CUB”) respectfully

submits these comments and limited protest pursuant to Rules 211 and 212 of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or “FERC”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18

C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.212 in response to the July 24, 2026 filing by the Midcontinent

Independent System Operator, Inc., (“MISO” as the Transmission Provider), on behalf of

American Transmission Company LLC, by its corporate manager, ATC Management Inc.

(collectively, “ATC” as the Transmission Owner) (“ATC Transmittal Letter”).

       While ATC’s proposed agreements would, if accepted, be an improvement on the status

quo, for the reasons below, CUB respectfully requests that the Commission find that the

Minimum Transmission Charge Agreement (MTCA) and four Amended Large Load Project

Commitment Agreements (“Amended LLPCAs”) (collectively, the “Agreements”) between ATC

and Wisconsin Electric Power Company (“WEPCO”) proposed in this docket:

   1. Are unjust and unreasonable as proposed because they lack adequate mechanisms to

       mitigate the risk of cost shifting between ATC’s transmission customers, which may

       result in unjust and unreasonable rates for transmission service.




                                                1
      2. Do not constitute template, precedential pro forma transmission cost allocation

         agreement(s) for new end-use large load customers in compliance with the Commission’s

         June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause (“Show Cause Order”). 1

         The MTCA and Amended LLPCAs should thus only be approved, if at all, subject to the

eventual approval of new pro forma transmission cost allocation agreements in satisfaction of the

Show Cause Order.

I.       BACKGROUND

     A. The Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin

         Wisconsin CUB was formed by the Wisconsin Legislature in 1979, 2 and is designated by

Wisconsin law to advocate on behalf of residential and small business public utility customers on

utility issues.3 The Wisconsin Legislature intended CUB to, among other things, represent the

rights of customers before regulatory agencies, including the Commission. 4

         Wisconsin CUB has an interest in ensuring that the rates Wisconsin customers pay for

transmission services are just and reasonable. The rates paid by Wisconsin’s residential and

small business customers will be affected by the Agreements proposed here. As the sole entity

designated by Wisconsin law to advocate for Wisconsin consumers, no other party adequately

represents the interests of Wisconsin CUB, and its participation in this matter is in the public

interest.




1
  Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., et al., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal
Power Act, 195 FERC ¶ 61,212 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”), dated June 18, 2026.
2
  Wis. Stat. Ch. 199
3
  Wis. Stat. § 196.315(1)
4
  Id.; Wis. Stat. § 199.02

                                                          2
     B. ATC’s existing cost allocation methods result in unreasonable shifts in large load
       transmission costs to other transmission customers.

        As part of its state-level duties, Wisconsin CUB has been deeply involved in proceedings

before the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (PSCW) examining retail large load tariffs,

including The Very Large Customer (VLC) and Bespoke Resources tariffs recently authorized

by the PSCW for WEPCO. 5 As part of those proceedings, the PSCW found that ATC’s current

zonal cost allocation method would likely result in a significant under-allocation of large load-

driven incremental transmission interconnection costs to the utility hosting the cost-causing large

load customer. 6 This would result in an unreasonable shifting of costs to other transmission

customers of ATC inconsistent with generally accepted cost-causation principles.

        ATC’s practice of recovering a current return on CWIP for all of its transmission projects

is, as the PSCW notes, “unique among transmission owners within MISO.” 7 Wisconsin CUB

believes this practice could be considered reasonable for traditional incremental transmission

investments, investments meant to ensure adequate and reliable transmission service for ATC’s

customers more generally. However, when applied to large load transmission interconnection

costs, the associated “[b]illion-dollar investments and gigawatt-scale loads have the potential to

shift tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in financing costs to the wrong customers.” 8

        Beyond the timing issue posed by the CWIP issue, ATC’s current rates are likely to result

in cost shifts, even under scenarios where large load customer usage materialized as expected.




5
  See Pub. Serv Comm’n. of Wisc. Order, Docket 6630-TE-113 (May 21, 2026) (PSCW Order).
6
  Comments of the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin to American Transmission Company LLC's
07/24/2026 tariff filing under ER26-3265, Accession # 20260814-5240 (“PSCW Comments”) at 3-5
7
  Id. at 7
8
  Id.

                                                    3
 In considering the reasonableness of the proposed agreements, the Commission must ensure that

ATC’s wholesale customer (WEPCO) will bear:

              1. The full incremental cost of all network upgrades necessary to interconnect the

                  large load customer, and

              2. The full cost of network transmission service separate from the incremental “but-

                  for” costs of large load interconnection.

          In its Show Cause Order, the Commission preliminarily found “that the minimum

contribution required… should be based on the level of jurisdictional transmission service (in

MW) requested by the Eligible Customer on behalf of the large load.” 9 Wisconsin CUB does not

disagree with this finding. But the reasonableness of any transmission charges proposed to

address large load costs must also address the unique nature of the incremental network upgrade

costs incurred to serve large loads.

          As the Commission observed in the Show Cause Order, large loads “can be more energy

intensive and geographically concentrated than traditional load, and exhibit different load

profiles and operational characteristics.” 10 As such, it would be reasonable to expect that the cost

of the incremental, “but-for” network upgrades associated with large loads on a dollars-per-

megawatt basis, would be different from the average embedded cost of traditional, historic

investments that make up the rest of ATC’s rate base. Moreover, given general inflationary

trends, as well as the “speed to market” pressures under which large load interconnections are

being undertaken, it would also be reasonable to expect that the cost of these network upgrades

to be higher, and perhaps substantially higher, than historic average embedded costs. Thus, any




9
    Show Cause Order at 52
10
     Id. at 33

                                                    4
 cost allocation method that relies on ATC’s standard Network Integration Transmission Service

(NITS) Rate set forth in Attachment O of the MISO Tariff is inappropriate for the purposes of

allocating the incremental “but-for” costs of large loads — the NITS rate, applicable to other

types of costs, would be too low. ATC’s traditional zonal rates (termed “Load Ratio Share”),

would thus under-recover the incremental costs associated with large loads.

          This is precisely what was revealed in the PSCW’s proceeding regarding WEPCO’s VLC

tariff. As the PSCW explained in its comments, the PSCW’s cost recovery analysis using actual

prospective customer data demonstrated the potential for a large load serving utility to never be

allocated the full incremental directly assignable costs associated with large load interconnection,

even under expected large load conditions. 11 Fundamentally, the electric demands and associated

supporting infrastructure investments are so large relative to traditional loads and investments

that any reasonable transmission rate aimed at reasonably recovering those incremental costs

must be derived from the actual costs incurred by the transmission company.

      C. A Standard Offer or Pro Forma Tariff Solution is necessary

          Wisconsin CUB’s experience in the PSCW’s large load cases to date has demonstrated

that the development of a comprehensive and detailed pro forma tariff solution for the allocation

of large load costs is a necessity. The Commission’s discussion of the need for a pro forma tariff

for large loads in its Show Cause Order is consistent with this experience.

          More fundamentally, a pro forma tariff for large loads would acknowledge the recent and

projected load growth driven by these large load customers for what it is – the emergence of a

new class of electric utility customers with service requirements and impacts on the utility

system that are distinct from existing classes of customers. Ad-hoc or individual customer



11
     PSCW Comments at 3-4

                                                 5
 contracts treat the customer in this new class as one-off exceptions, which the Commission’s

Show Cause Order acknowledges is not the case. The creation of a pro forma tariff allows for the

regulation of rates and rules for very-large customers according to the same regulatory principles

that guide the setting of rates for all other customer classes, while increasing transparency and

consistency of the rate-setting process. That is, through the establishment and application of fair,

just, reasonable, free from undue discrimination.

II.        COMMENTS

       A. The proposed MTCA fails to address cost shifting among transmission customers

           Under the proposed MTCA would assess WEPCO a Minimum Transmission Charge

associated with the underlying large load customer (Microsoft). ATC states 12:


           To calculate the Minimum Transmission Charge, ATC shall determine whether
           WEPCo paid the Network Rate through Schedule 9-ATC for 100% of the MW
           value of the Requested Transmission Capacity Schedule for each month. In the
           event that WEPCo did not pay 100% of the MW value of the Requested
           Transmission Capacity Schedule in any given month, it will be invoiced under the
           MTCA at the Network Rate for the difference between the Schedule 9-ATC
           amount and the Requested Transmission Capacity. In other words, under the
           MTCA, WEPCo is committing to pay 100% of Network Service for transmission
           capacity it requests ATC to construct to serve the Microsoft data center campus –
           either through Schedule 9-ATC or through the Minimum Transmission Charge.
           In basing the Minimum Transmission Charge on any shortfall in the Schedule 9 MW

volumes relative to the Requested Transmission Capacity demands, ATC’s proposal aims to

address the billing determinant issue associated with large load uncertainty, specifically periods

where actual large load demand falls short of the projected demand underling the incremental

transmission capacity requested by WEPCO to serve Microsoft. However, ATC also proposes to

bill the Minimum Transmission Charge at a rate equal to ATC’s overall network rate rather than



12
     ATC Transmittal Letter at 6

                                                   6
 at a rate derived from the actual incremental network upgrade costs incurred to serve Microsoft’s

load. As discussed above, applying the NITS rate to large load demands is likely to result in

under-recovery from the large load serving utility.

        Moreover, as also noted previously, there are two essential categories of costs for which

the Commission must ensure reasonable cost recovery: Incremental “but-for” large load network

costs, and “traditional” network costs. ATC’s proposal does not appear to distinguish between

the two. If anything, given that the Minimum Transmission Charge Liability Cap would be set

based on the “aggregate incremental revenue requirement for the T-D Project facilities over their

useful life,” 13 ATC’s proposal seems to be pegged only to what it identifies as the incremental

costs, without consideration of whether the large load customer’s share of revenue requirements

associated with the rest of the transmission network are also recovered from WEPCO.

     B. The Proposed Agreements Lack Adequate Transparency

        ATC states that it “initiated the Best Value Planning (“BVP”) process in which ATC, in

collaboration with WEPCo, determined the most cost-effective, optimal solution to serve

[Microsoft’s] load.” 14 One would presume that the results of the BVP process, the “Best Value

Plan” 15 would serve as the cost basis for the Amended LLPCAs. However, that does not appear

to be the case as no BVP Report is included with any of the Amended LLPCAs. 16 As such it is

unclear what the basis for the costs covered by the Amended LLPCAs is, and whether the terms

of the Amended LLPCAs are sufficient to protect against stranded assets during the during

construction or if a project is cancelled prior to its in-service date.




13
   ATC Transmittal Letter at 6
14
   ATC Transmittal Letter at 3
15
   MTCA Agreement at 2
16
   See Amended LLPCAs Exhibit B3

                                                   7
            As previously noted, the proposed Minimum Transmission Charge is capped at the

Minimum Transmission Charge Liability Cap. ATC defines the Minimum Transmission Charge

Liability Cap as:

           Customer’s aggregate, cumulative Minimum Transmission Charge payment
           obligation under this MTCA and Customer Load Project Schedule 9 Charge under
           the MISO Tariff shall not exceed an amount equal to the aggregate incremental
           revenue requirement for the Transmission Project over its useful life calculated
           utilizing ATC’s formula rate in Attachment O of the MISO Tariff in effect as of
           the Effective Date (the “Minimum Transmission Charge Liability Cap”).
           While ATC provides a dollar estimate of the Minimum Transmission Charge Liability

Cap in Exhibit F to the MTCA, no information is provided regarding what underlying

transmission system components and associated costs are used to calculate the cap. As such, it is

unclear whether the proposed charges would actually result in WEPCO paying 100% of the costs

associated with the transmission capacity it has requested ATC to construct to serve the

Microsoft data center campus.

       C. The Proposed Agreements Should Not Be Deemed a New, Pro Forma Cost Recovery
          Agreements in Satisfaction of the Show Cause Order.

           ATC claims that “[t]he protections instituted by the Amended LLPCAs and MTCA are

just and reasonable, consistent with Commission precedent, responsive to the Commission’s

recent Order to Show Cause on large loads, fair to the Parties, and fair to and protective of

ATC’s other wholesale customers.” 17 CUB disagrees. As discussed above, ratemaking

infirmities – including the lack of transparency in allocation methods – mean that the proposed

agreements fail to address “additional transparency concerning the Network Upgrade costs to

provide transmission service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads” and fail to “mitigate




17
     ATC Transmittal Letter at 7

                                                  8
 the risk of cost shifting among transmission customers” as directed in the Show Cause Order. 18

Additionally, CUB agrees with the Data Center Coalition (DCC) that ATC’s filings in this

docket fail to satisfy the requirements set forth in the Show Cause Order as they are not the result

any stakeholder process. 19

III.       CONCLUSION

           While ATC’s proposal would likely be an improvement over the status quo, because it

would lock in a cost allocation mechanism for Wisconsin’s first hyperscale data center customer

for the long term, the Commission must ensure that it is just and reasonable. For the reasons set

forth above, CUB requests that the Commission find that the Agreements between ATC and

Wisconsin Electric Power Company (“WEPCO”) proposed in this docket:

       1. Are unjust and unreasonable as proposed because they lack adequate mechanisms to

           mitigate the risk of cost shifting between ATC’s transmission customers.

       2. Do not constitute template, precedential pro forma transmission cost allocation

           agreement(s) for new end-use large load customers in compliance with the Commission’s

           June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause (“Show Cause Order”).

       3. To the extent the MTCA and Amended LLPCAs are approved, approval should be

           subject to the eventual approval of new pro forma transmission cost allocation

           agreements in satisfaction of the Show Cause Order that would supersede the MTCA and

           Amended LLPCAs.
